 moved back into focus as the energy major reported record production for its latest quarter and paired the update with another increase to its dividend, drawing a wave of fresh commentary across financial media. The combination of rising output and a steady approach to cash distributions kept the name near the center of the sector conversation even as crude prices stayed soft. As one of the largest publicly traded energy companies in the world, ExxonMobil tends to set the tone for how the market reads the wider oil and gas space. When the company reports, peers and suppliers alike are watched for readacross, and the latest update arrived with enough detail on volumes, spending and distributions to keep attention firmly fixed. Renewed interest also reflects the backdrop. With soft crude pricing weighing on the group, the market has leaned harder on which operators can keep growing volumes and defending cash flow through the cycle. ExxonMobil used its update to underline both themes, giving traders a clear checkpoint on how the major is navigating a demanding stretch for oil. The central event drawing eyes was a quarterly report that showed output reaching fresh highs even as the price of crude eased from earlier levels. The company framed the period as evidence that its lower-cost barrels and expanding projects can keep volumes climbing regardless of where oil trades on any given day. Reporting periods for the energy majors tend to be closely parsed because the segment swings with commodity prices, and the market looks for signs that a company can sustain earnings through softer stretches. ExxonMobil leaned on growing production from its most advantaged assets to argue that it can keep delivering even as crude stays under pressure. Framed this way, the update reads less as a single headline figure and more as a progress check on a multi-year effort to lift volumes from a handful of flagship developments. The timing mattered too, arriving while the broad market measured by the S&P 500 stayed absorbed in technology earnings and heavy spending on data-center power, leaving energy names to trade largely on their own merits. The energy space has spent recent sessions pulled in several directions at once. Crude oil has been soft and under pressure, while natural gas and liquefied natural gas themes have stayed active and electricity demand tied to data centers has lent support to power-linked names. An integrated major such as ExxonMobil sits across many of these crosscurrents at once. Softer crude has sharpened the focus on cost discipline and volume growth, since operators that can keep expanding cheap barrels are better placed to weather a weaker price environment. That dynamic has put a premium on scale, low breakeven costs and a deep inventory of projects, all areas where the company argues it stands apart. Sentiment across the group has also been shaped by the steady climb in global energy demand and the push to balance conventional output with lower-carbon ventures. Each shift in those conditions tends to move the whole sector rather than any single name, keeping the broader conversation lively and the majors firmly in view. ExxonMobil operates across the full energy value chain, spanning upstream exploration and production, refining and a large chemicals arm. That integrated structure gives the company a footprint that stretches across many countries and lets different segments offset one another as commodity prices move through their cycles. The upstream business centers on finding and producing crude oil and natural gas, and it has become the engine of the company's growth story thanks to a handful of advantaged developments. Downstream, a network of refineries turns those barrels into fuels and lubricants, while the chemicals arm converts feedstocks into materials used across countless everyday products. This breadth is often framed as a source of resilience. When crude prices soften, refining and chemicals can cushion the blow, and when oil firms, the upstream arm carries the momentum. That balance has long defined how the market reads the company and helps explain why its updates draw such close attention. The scale of the operation also gives ExxonMobil a reach that few rivals can match, from deepwater projects to sprawling refining complexes. That size brings both advantages, through cost efficiency and bargaining weight, and scrutiny, since the company's moves ripple widely across the energy landscape. Two developments sit at the heart of the company's growth story and help explain why the stock features so prominently within the wider US Oil and Gas Stocks that traders follow when gauging sentiment across the energy theme. The Permian Basin in the United States and the offshore fields of Guyana have become the twin engines lifting volumes to fresh highs. In the Permian, the company has leaned on a large acreage position and a focus on drilling efficiency to pull more barrels from each well at a lower cost. That low-breakeven profile is often described as a way to keep output growing even when crude trades softly, since the economics still work at prices that would strain higher-cost operators. Offshore Guyana, a string of discoveries has turned a frontier region into one of the fastest-growing sources of new supply anywhere in the world. Successive production vessels have come online, each adding fresh capacity, and the company has pointed to this ramp as a central reason its volumes keep setting records. Together, these two assets anchor a long runway of growth that sets the company apart from peers more reliant on mature fields. The market treats progress across both as a key gauge of whether the major can keep lifting output while much of the wider industry keeps spending steady. title: Buy CVX and XOM Amid Solid Q3 Earnings and Surging Crude Oil Prices - The Globe and Mail
content: Crude oil prices have soared this year buoyed by geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East, with no signs of abatement. Year to date, the U.S. benchmark — the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude future price climbed 77.7%, while the international benchmark — the Brent crude future price jumped 84.6%. In  October alone, WTI and Brent crude oil surged 15% and 13%, respectively. WTI is currently hovering around $103 per barrel, and Brent is hovering around $114 per barrel. Crude oil prices are likely to remain elevated due to growing geopolitical conflicts globally. Consequently, stock prices of crude oil explorers and producers have surged in 2026. Here, we recommend two crude oil exploration behemoths with a top Zacks Rank for investment.  These are: Chevron Corp.CVX and ExxonMobil Holdings Corp.XOM. On Oct. 30, both companies reported solid third-quarter 2026 earnings results and as a result, recorded their all-time high stock prices. Both stocks currently sport a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy). CVX’s downstream operations recorded earnings of $4.9 billion, compared with $1.1 billion a year earlier. The substantial improvement primarily reflected stronger margins on refined product sales. In the reported quarter, CVX generated $16 billion in operating cash flow compared with $9.4 billion a year earlier. Free cash flow surged to $12 billion from $4.9 billion a year ago. On Oct. 30, the stock price of CVX touched an all-time high of $236.48. Chevron has an expected revenue and earnings growth rate of 28.2% and more than 100%, respectively, for the current year. title: Why Did MO, GILD, XOM Stocks Surge To 52-Week Highs Last Week? - TradingView
content: Altria Group (MO), Gilead Sciences (GILD) and ExxonMobil (XOM) stocks ascended to fresh 52-week highs on Friday after strong third-quarter results, improved earnings outlooks and higher shareholder returns boosted investor confidence. Strong tobacco pricing, growing HIV drug sales and improved refining margins supported gains across the three companies. Altria and ExxonMobil stocks gained 1% and 2%, respectively, while Gilead Sciences stock climbed 3%. Altria Gains After Earnings Beat And Higher Outlook Altria stock reached a record high of $79.81 after the tobacco company delivered better-than-expected third-quarter (Q3) 2026 results. Adjusted earnings came in at $1.52 per share, narrowly exceeding Wall Street's $1.51 estimate, as per Fiscal.ai. Revenue, excluding excise taxes, increased 3.6% from a year earlier to $5.44 billion. The company raised its 2026 earnings forecast to $5.66 - $5.74 per share and increased its stock buyback plan by another $1 billion. UBS raised its price target on MO to $83 from $79 and kept a ‘Buy’ rating. Morgan Stanley lifted its price target to $77 from $71 but maintained an ‘Equal Weight’ rating, citing weakness in traditional cigarette sales. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the stock remained in ‘neutral’ territory. Gilead Sciences stock touched an all-time high of $175.65 after exceeding Q3 revenue and earnings expectations. Its HIV business remained a major growth engine, supported by demand for treatments such as Biktarvy and its pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) portfolio. The company raised its full-year HIV business growth guidance to 12%, up from its earlier estimate of 9% to 10%. Scotiabank raised its Gilead price target to $200 from $177 and kept an ‘Outperform’ rating, suggesting a 18% upside possibility from the stock’s last close. Truist also increased its target to $181 from $158 while maintaining a ‘Buy’ rating. Retail sentiment around the stock improved to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’. ExxonMobil Rides On Refining Strength And Higher Dividends ExxonMobil stock also hit a record high of $188.50 after the energy producer reported adjusted Q3 earnings of $4.23 per share, above the $4.03 analyst consensus. Revenue totaled $110.50 billion. ExxonMobil's Energy Products division saw adjusted earnings rise to $9.05 billion, more than doubling from the previous quarter. Higher refining profits and full use of its U.S. Gulf Coast facilities helped drive the growth. Meanwhile, oil production from Guyana's Stabroek Block passed the 1-billion-barrel mark. The company raised its quarterly dividend by 3.8% to $1.07 per share and plans to continue its $20 billion share-repurchase program in 2027. Retail sentiment around the stock shifted to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’. So far this year, MO, GILD and XOM stocks have gained between 35% and 55%. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. Cybersecurity stocks have emerged as some of the biggest winners of the artificial intelligence boom in 2026, with investors betting that the same technology transforming businesses is also creating a new wave of security threats. Okta Inc. (OKTA), CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. (CRWD) and Palo Alto Networks Inc. (PLTR) are up 141%, 114% and 99%, respectively, through Oct. 30. The First Trust NASDAQ Cybersecurity ETF (CIBR) is also up nearly 40%, far ahead of the Nasdaq 100’s roughly 11% gain. CrowdStrike shares closed more than 4% lower in Friday’s regular trading session, Palo Alto Networks shares fell nearly 4%, while Okta shares fell over 6%. According to IO Fund, the first major driver behind the rally is the growing use of AI in cyberattacks and the expanding attack surface companies now have to defend. CrowdStrike’s 2026 Global Threat Report, cited by IO Fund, found that AI-enabled adversaries increased their operations by 89% in 2025. IBM’s research shows that one in four security breaches is now AI-enabled, with those incidents costing roughly $6 million on average, versus a $4.99 million global average. The threat is also pushing companies to increase spending. IO Fund cited IBM data showing that 85% of organizations plan to raise security spending after learning about the cyber capabilities of frontier AI models, up from 64% in 2025. The shift is becoming particularly important as companies deploy increasingly autonomous AI agents that can write code, access systems and perform tasks with limited human intervention. The firm also pointed to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s warning about the difficulty of securing increasingly capable AI systems: “I no longer think we’re gonna be able to just patch all the bugs,” Altman said during a speech at Stanford Graduate School of Business last month. IO Fund said Gartner expects spending on platforms designed to secure AI systems to climb from about $3 billion in 2026 to $7.7 billion in 2028, suggesting the emerging threat could translate into a substantial new security spending cycle. The other major trend identified by IO Fund is happening inside corporate security departments, which is, customers are increasingly consolidating their spending across broader cybersecurity platforms rather than buying a growing number of point solutions. CrowdStrike’s results offer one indication of the trend, the firm said, adding that CrowdStrike’s annual recurring revenue from its Falcon Flex offering topped $2.2 billion, up 101% year over year, while 51% of its subscription customers now use six or more modules. The firm added that Palo Alto Networks is seeing a similar shift. IO Fund noted that the company added roughly 220 platformization deals in its fiscal fourth quarter (Q4), more than double the pace from two years earlier. Net revenue retention among platformized customers exceeded 120%, while Prisma AIRS, its AI security platform, surpassed $100 million in annual recurring revenue. IO Fund added that AI may not simply create demand for a new category of security products, but it could also accelerate spending with vendors that can secure multiple parts of an enterprise’s infrastructure. IO Fund estimates CrowdStrike’s revenue could grow at a 23% compound annual rate through fiscal 2029, more than twice Gartner’s projected 11% annual growth for the overall cybersecurity market. Okta and Tenable are expected to grow at roughly 10% and 7%, respectively. title: Exxon's Refining Profits Soared—Did Chevron Get the Same Windfall? - MarketBeat
content:
The biggest question for investors is not whether Exxon's refining business has been thriving thanks in large part to record crack spreads amid the Iran war, but how much of the earnings from these operations reached the company's bottom line, and how long that benefit is likely to last. Since competitor Chevron NYSE: CVX reported its Q3 2026 earnings results on the same day, it provides a useful point of comparison. Ultimately, Exxon's refining and marketing earnings have surpassed its upstream earnings, but the favorable mix may not continue forever. Exxon posted its largest year-to-date (YTD) refining operational performance ever, contributing to $17.5 billion in adjusted Q3 2026 earnings. Breaking down these earnings by segment shows just how dramatically refining has impacted the company's overall performance. The company's Energy Products segment includes its refining and marketing operations; this portion of Exxon's business reached $9 billion in adjusted earnings for Q3, more than double what it was last year at this time. Meanwhile, the company's upstream business, including its core exploration and production operations, came in at $7.3 billion in adjusted earnings for the quarter, down from $9.2 billion in Q2 2026. This decline was substantially wider than Exxon had indicated in its pre-earnings report. In other words, Exxon's Energy Products segment became the company's largest earnings generator for the company this quarter. While this has been a boon for the company, it leaves it exposed if fuel margins should fade. At the same time, the company still produced about 4.5 million barrels of oil equivalent per day—though this is about flat on a sequential basis, it nonetheless indicates that there are not necessarily major issues with Exxon's upstream operations for investors to worry about. For this firm, production remained the largest contributor to overall earnings. Chevron's upstream operations generated about $5.7 billion in reported earnings for Q3, while its downstream operations (including refining) yielded $4.9 billion. The company also saw a heavy downward swing for its upstream earnings compared to Q2 2026, as the figure fell from $8.2 billion at that time. Notably, though, downstream earnings was essentially flat from Q2 to Q3 2026. International downstream earnings actually declined on a sequential basis, offsetting gains made in the domestic portion of Chevron's business, which processed about 1.1 million barrels per day at about 98% utilization. Russian diesel waivers and the potential for normalized Gulf shipping may help to ease the tight fuel supply in the months to come. Margins may still remain elevated, however, if geopolitical stressors continue or if refinery output from Russia remains limited. There is also strong seasonal demand to look ahead to, although a historically heavy El Niño may throw off predictions for energy usage. If margins normalize, investors will probably look more to the pace at which these firms buy shares back and how they spend their capital. Both enter the end of the year with significant capacity to generate cash. Exxon has a $20-billion 2027 buyback plan that seems to suggest management is confident the company will continue to print cash, as well as an investment program that should help to improve refinery efficiency. Chevron bought back $2.5 billion in shares last quarter, slightly lower than the previous period, but it is pushing more money toward upstream development. Investors should keep an eye on buyback plans and how they compare to distributions that are tied to temporary commodity market conditions. Additionally, diesel inventories and Russian export volumes will help to assess the impact of global conditions on both companies' margins. Alongside others in the oil and gas space, there are plenty of reasons for investors to be pleased with recent performance, although the big question is whether these companies can maintain their momentum. content: ExxonMobil reported year-on-year sales growth in Q3 2026, but missed Wall Street’s revenue and profit expectations. Management attributed the quarter’s performance to strong refining margins and disciplined cost control, despite a modest decline in oil production. CEO Darren Woods highlighted that investments, such as the Beaumont refinery expansion, have “paid for themselves in about three years” and are critical in meeting global demand. The company benefited from its integrated value chain, especially in refining and trading, as supply disruptions and geopolitical tensions tightened global markets. Is now the time to buy XOM? Those are unscripted and can often highlight topics that management teams would rather avoid or topics where the answer is complicated. Here is what has caught our attention. Devin McDermott (Morgan Stanley): Asked about long-term refining strategy beyond recent expansions. CEO Darren Woods explained the focus on leveraging technology and existing assets for high-value product yields, with plans for further reconfigurations at U.S. sites. Neil Mehta (Goldman Sachs): Inquired about the sustainability of share buybacks and dividend growth if oil prices fall. Woods and CFO Neil Hansen emphasized their strategy to maintain consistent shareholder returns through cycles, supported by a strong balance sheet. Arun Jayaram (J.P. Morgan): Sought clarity on the company’s global gas strategy and recent moves in Papua New Guinea and Mozambique. Woods detailed the importance of operatorship and technology leadership in pursuing LNG growth and operational excellence. Steve Richardson (Evercore): Probed for updates on Permian Basin production cadence and technology deployment. Woods highlighted early achievements in automated drilling and secondary recovery, with expectations for further improvements over time. Biraj Borkhataria (RBC): Asked about the timing and hurdles for final investment decision in Mozambique’s LNG project. Woods expressed optimism for year-end approval, citing increased efficiency from integrating upstream assets.
